questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a hypopigmented patch on his left forearm with loss of sensation to pin-prick. Slit skin smear from the lesion is negative. Biopsy shows epithelioid granulomas with lymphocytic infiltrate around dermal nerves. No bacilli seen on Fite-Faraco stain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) presents with a single or few hypopigmented anaesthetic patches, negative SSS, and biopsy showing well-formed epithelioid granulomas destroying dermal nerves with no bacilli. The strong cell-mediated immunity results in a localized paucibacillary disease.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man presents with painful genital ulcers that are soft, non-indurated, with ragged edges and a necrotic base. Inguinal lymphadenopathy is present with fluctuant bubo. Gram stain of the ulcer discharge shows 'school of fish' pattern. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi presents with painful soft ulcers with ragged undermined edges and suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). The Gram stain shows gram-negative coccobacilli in 'school of fish' or 'railroad track' arrangement.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of tense blisters on normal-appearing and erythematous skin, predominantly on flexural areas. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition at the dermo-epidermal junction. ELISA for BPAG2 (BP180) is positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by tense subepidermal blisters, negative Nikolsky sign, linear IgG and C3 at DEJ on DIF, and antibodies against BPAG1 (BP230) and BPAG2 (BP180). It is the most common autoimmune blistering disorder.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with a butterfly-shaped erythema over the malar region sparing the nasolabial folds, oral ulcers, and joint pain. Investigations show pancytopenia, proteinuria, and positive ANA (1:640). Which antibody is most specific for her condition?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibodies are highly specific for SLE (specificity ~99%) though sensitivity is low (~25-30%). Anti-dsDNA is sensitive and correlates with disease activity/nephritis. Anti-histone is seen in drug-induced lupus. Anti-Ro/SSA is seen in subacute cutaneous lupus and neonatal lupus.

questions.q: A 55-year-old diabetic man presents with a well-demarcated, painful, erythematous swelling on his left lower leg that is warm to touch. The infection is superficial, affecting the dermis and upper subcutaneous tissue. There are no bullae or crepitus. What is the most likely diagnosis and the drug of choice?
questions.exp: Cellulitis affects deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissue and is typically caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. In diabetics, Staphylococcus is more common, making flucloxacillin (anti-staphylococcal penicillin) the drug of choice. Erysipelas has a sharper border and is more superficial.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with whitish plaques on the buccal mucosa that cannot be wiped off. KOH mount shows pseudohyphae and budding yeast cells. He is on long-term inhaled corticosteroids for asthma. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Oral itraconazole 200 mg daily for 2 weeks
questions.exp: Oral candidiasis (thrush) in patients on inhaled corticosteroids is treated with nystatin oral suspension (swish and swallow) or clotrimazole troches as first-line topical therapy. Systemic fluconazole is reserved for refractory cases or immunocompromised patients.

questions.q: A 14-year-old girl presents with multiple flat-topped polygonal violaceous papules on her wrists and ankles. She complains of intense itching. Oral mucosa shows a white lace-like pattern. Biopsy shows saw-tooth acanthosis, wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, and band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ with civatte bodies. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lichen planus presents with the 6 P's: Pruritic, Planar (flat-topped), Purple, Polygonal, Papules, and Plaques. Wickham's striae are white lacy lines on oral mucosa. Histology shows saw-tooth acanthosis, wedge hypergranulosis, band-like lichenoid infiltrate, and Civatte (colloid) bodies.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery-white scales on the elbows and knees. Auspitz sign is positive. Nail examination reveals pitting, onycholysis, and subungual hyperkeratosis. The drug most likely to cause exacerbation of this condition is:
questions.exp: Psoriasis can be exacerbated by lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials (chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine), NSAIDs, and withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids. Methotrexate, cyclosporine, and acitretin are actually used to treat psoriasis.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with multiple painless genital papules. Examination reveals soft, skin-colored, cauliflower-like lesions around the vulva and perianal region. Which HPV types are most commonly responsible for this presentation?
questions.exp: Condyloma acuminata (genital warts) are caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11, which have low oncogenic potential. HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk types associated with cervical carcinoma, penile carcinoma, and Bowen's disease/bowenoid papulosis.

questions.q: A 65-year-old woman presents with painless, progressive thickening of the skin over the face, neck, and extremities over 5 years. She has Raynaud's phenomenon, dysphagia, and dyspnoea. HRCT shows basal fibrosis. ANA is positive. Which antibody is most specifically associated with pulmonary hypertension in this condition?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc/CREST syndrome) and carries an increased risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension. Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc and pulmonary fibrosis. Anti-RNA polymerase III is associated with renal crisis.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child develops multiple vesicles in different stages (macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts) over the trunk and face over 3 days, following contact with an affected classmate. The lesions spare the palms and soles. Mother reports fever and malaise. What is the antiviral drug indicated for a healthy child with this condition?
opts: Oral acyclovir 20 mg/kg QID for 5 days
questions.exp: Varicella (chickenpox) in a healthy immunocompetent child is self-limiting and acyclovir is NOT routinely recommended. It may be considered in adolescents, adults, and high-risk groups (immunocompromised, chronic skin/lung disease, those on corticosteroids). IV acyclovir is used for varicella pneumonia, encephalitis, or severe disseminated disease.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man on long-term dapsone for leprosy develops sudden onset pallor, jaundice, dark urine, and fatigue. CBC shows haemoglobin 6 g/dL with reticulocytosis. Peripheral smear shows Heinz bodies and bite cells. What is the mechanism?
opts: Immune-mediated haemolysis due to IgG antibodies
G6PD deficiency leading to oxidative haemolysis
Bone marrow suppression causing aplastic anaemia
questions.exp: Dapsone is an oxidant drug that can cause haemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency. G6PD-deficient RBCs cannot regenerate NADPH needed to neutralize oxidative stress, leading to Heinz body formation (denatured Hb) and haemolysis. This is the most common serious adverse effect of dapsone in susceptible individuals.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent papule with rolled borders and telangiectasias on his nose. He has a long history of sun exposure. Dermoscopy shows arborizing vessels and spoke-wheel structures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer, typically presenting on sun-exposed areas as a pearly papule/nodule with rolled borders, telangiectasias, and central ulceration (rodent ulcer). Dermoscopy shows arborizing (branching) vessels, spoke-wheel areas, and large blue-grey ovoid nests.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman is being treated for onychomycosis. She is also on oral contraceptive pills. Which antifungal agent has a significant drug interaction with her contraceptive pill?
questions.exp: Griseofulvin induces hepatic CYP enzymes (particularly CYP3A4), which accelerates the metabolism of oral contraceptive pills, reducing their efficacy. This is a well-known drug interaction requiring alternative contraception. Terbinafine has minimal CYP interactions. Azoles like itraconazole and fluconazole inhibit CYP3A4, potentially increasing OCP levels.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in the T5-T6 dermatomal distribution on his left side. He had chickenpox as a child. What complication can occur even after complete resolution of the skin lesions?
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is the most common complication of herpes zoster, occurring in 10-15% of patients, with risk increasing with age. It is defined as pain persisting more than 90 days after rash onset. Ramsay Hunt syndrome occurs with zoster of the geniculate ganglion affecting CN VII.

questions.q: A biopsy from a patient with dermatitis herpetiformis shows subepidermal vesicles with neutrophilic microabscesses at the dermal papillary tips. Direct immunofluorescence reveals granular deposits at the DEJ. Which immunoglobulin is deposited?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis is characterized by granular IgA deposits at the dermo-epidermal junction (specifically at the dermal papillary tips) on direct immunofluorescence. This is the gold standard for diagnosis. The condition is associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy (celiac disease).

questions.q: A 40-year-old man from Bihar presents with an ulcerated nodule on his face that slowly expanded over 6 months. He has significant weight loss and epistaxis. Biopsy shows diffuse histiocytic infiltrate with intracellular organisms (amastigotes). What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: This describes post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) or visceral leishmaniasis. In India, liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome) is now the first-line treatment for visceral leishmaniasis due to widespread antimonial (SSG) resistance in Bihar. Miltefosine is an oral alternative.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman develops a herald patch on the trunk followed by multiple oval erythematous patches with a collarette of scale arranged in a 'Christmas tree' pattern along skin lines of cleavage. The condition is self-limiting. Which virus has been implicated in its pathogenesis?
questions.exp: Pityriasis rosea (PR) has been linked to reactivation of Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) and HHV-7. It classically presents with a herald patch followed by a secondary eruption of oval lesions following Langer's lines (Christmas tree pattern). It is self-limiting, resolving in 6-8 weeks.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man develops painful swelling and redness of his ear canal, with otitis externa, facial nerve palsy, and loss of taste from the anterior 2/3 of tongue after herpes zoster. What is this syndrome called and which ganglion is involved?
questions.exp: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) results from VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of CN VII. Clinically, it presents with a painful vesicular eruption in the ear canal/pinna, peripheral facial nerve palsy, and loss of taste in anterior 2/3 tongue. Treatment is with acyclovir and corticosteroids.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a chronic wound on the sole of his foot that has been present for 2 years. He has Type 2 diabetes and peripheral neuropathy. Examination reveals a punched-out ulcer over the pressure point at the first metatarsal head, surrounded by callus, with no pain. What type of ulcer is this?
questions.exp: Diabetic neuropathic ulcers (mal perforans) occur at pressure points (metatarsal heads, heel) due to sensory neuropathy. Features: painless, punched-out margins, surrounded by callus, over bony prominences, good pulses. Venous ulcers occur above medial malleolus; arterial ulcers are painful with absent pulses.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man presents with depigmented macules with distinct margins and no sensory loss. Wood's lamp examination shows brilliant white fluorescence of the patches. There is no family history. Which disease must be differentiated from vitiligo in this patient?
questions.exp: Vitiligo must be differentiated from tuberculoid leprosy which also presents with hypopigmented macules. Key differentiating features: leprosy macules have impaired sensation (hypoaesthesia), impaired sweating, and show no fluorescence on Wood's lamp (vitiligo shows chalk-white/brilliant white fluorescence). Skin biopsy and SSS help confirm leprosy.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with episodic urticaria lasting 6 weeks. Examination reveals wheals that last less than 24 hours and resolve without scarring. He has no identifiable trigger. Serum IgE levels are elevated. What is the first-line pharmacological treatment?
questions.exp: The first-line treatment for chronic spontaneous urticaria is second-generation H1 antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine, fexofenadine, loratadine) at licensed doses. They are preferred over first-generation antihistamines due to better tolerability. Omalizumab is used for antihistamine-refractory chronic urticaria (third-line). Systemic corticosteroids are avoided for long-term use.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant presents with intensely pruritic erythematous papules and vesicles on the cheeks, forehead, and extensor surfaces of limbs. The lesions are weeping and crusting. Mother has seasonal allergic rhinitis. What is the expected finding on serum investigation?
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis presents in infancy with involvement of face and extensor surfaces, progressing to flexural areas in older children. It is associated with elevated total serum IgE and peripheral eosinophilia, reflecting the underlying Th2-skewed immune response. Family history of atopy (asthma, rhinitis, eczema) is common.

questions.q: A 38-year-old HIV-positive man with CD4 count of 80 cells/µL presents with multiple brown to violaceous plaques on the lower extremities. Biopsy shows proliferating spindle cells with vascular spaces and extravasated red blood cells. Which organism is causally associated with this condition?
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma in AIDS patients is causally associated with HHV-8 (Human Herpesvirus 8, also called Kaposi Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus/KSHV). It is an AIDS-defining illness. Histology shows spindle cells, vascular spaces, inflammatory cells, and extravasated erythrocytes. Treatment includes HAART therapy.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman undergoes patch testing for suspected contact dermatitis. The test is applied for 48 hours and read at 72-96 hours. A positive reaction shows erythema, oedema, and vesicles at the test site only (not the surrounding skin). What type of hypersensitivity is being tested?
questions.exp: Patch testing detects Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity, also called cell-mediated or T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity. The reaction occurs 48-96 hours after antigen application, mediated by sensitized CD4+ T cells (Th1) releasing cytokines. This underlies allergic contact dermatitis. The test is standardized using the European Standard Series.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman is prescribed isotretinoin for nodulocystic acne. She is sexually active. Which precaution is absolutely mandatory before starting and during isotretinoin therapy?
opts: Monthly pregnancy test and use of two forms of contraception
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen (Category X). Before initiation, a negative pregnancy test is mandatory. Two forms of contraception must be used for at least 1 month before, throughout, and 1 month after treatment. Monthly pregnancy tests are required. This is governed by the iPLEDGE programme in the USA and similar programmes globally.

questions.q: A 75-year-old woman with a history of pemphigus vulgaris being treated with high-dose prednisolone develops a new burning and stinging erythematous erosion on the perioral area and perineum. KOH mount shows pseudohyphae. What is the most common opportunistic fungal infection in this setting?
questions.exp: Candida albicans is the most common opportunistic fungal pathogen in immunocompromised patients on systemic corticosteroids. It thrives in moist occluded areas (mucocutaneous junctions, intertriginous areas). Patients on long-term immunosuppressive therapy for bullous disorders are particularly susceptible.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man presents with a painless indurated chancre on his penis for 10 days. The chancre has a clean base with a cartilaginous feel on palpation. Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged, rubbery, and non-tender. Dark-field microscopy shows motile spirochaetes. What is the VDRL/RPR expected to show at this stage?
opts: Always negative as it only becomes positive in secondary syphilis
VDRL is contraindicated in primary syphilis
questions.exp: In primary syphilis, VDRL/RPR may be non-reactive in 25-30% of cases, especially in early infection, due to the prozone phenomenon or window period. Dark-field microscopy is the gold standard for diagnosis at this stage. VDRL becomes positive in secondary syphilis and titre correlates with disease activity.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs a liquid nitrogen cryotherapy on a seborrhoeic keratosis. She informs the patient that blistering is expected. Which statement about cryosurgery is correct?
opts: The freeze-thaw mechanism causes ischaemic necrosis and direct cellular injury
Melanocytes are more resistant to cryodamage than keratinocytes
Carbon dioxide snow (dry ice) achieves a lower temperature than liquid nitrogen
A single freeze-thaw cycle is adequate for all benign lesions
questions.exp: Cryosurgery works via direct cellular injury (ice crystal formation, osmotic damage) and indirect vascular injury causing ischaemic necrosis after thawing. Melanocytes are more sensitive than keratinocytes to cryodamage, explaining post-treatment hypopigmentation. Liquid nitrogen (-196°C) achieves much lower temperatures than CO2 snow (-78.5°C).

questions.q: A 30-year-old leprosy patient on multi-drug therapy (MDT) develops painful erythematous nodules over the face and extremities associated with fever, arthralgia, and lymphadenopathy. The nodules appear suddenly and last for days to weeks. What type of lepra reaction is this?
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL) is a Type 2 lepra reaction occurring in lepromatous (LL) and borderline lepromatous (BL) leprosy. It is an immune-complex mediated (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction presenting with tender nodules, fever, and systemic symptoms. Treatment is thalidomide (males/post-menopausal women) or clofazimine + steroids.
